newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's big insurers warily watch EMU turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Japan's big insurers warily watch EMU turmoil.

text.p: As Europe grapples with the vexed question of economic and monetary union, Japan's cash-rich life insurers are warily watching for the latest spin on what they still essentially view as a good investment.
"The situation is still unstable, but we still regard it as a good opportunity," said Takashi Kawashima, a manager in the investment planning division of Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance.

Insurance company managers in Tokyo said they were anxious about which countries will actually join the European economic and monetary union (EMU) in the 1999 "first round" and whether it will meet the deadline, but added they remained hopeful.

On Monday, Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher was quoted by a newspaper as saying he was not sure the EMU would start on time, but fellow member Ernst Welteke later said he did not see any need to think about such a delay.
A manager in the international department at Asahi Mutual Life Insurance dismissed Kuehbacher's comments as "mere noise".
"This is a question of Europe's future identity, so there will be no deviation from this course," he said. "Considering a failure scenario for the EMU now makes no sense."

An official in the international investment department of Nippon Life Insurance, Japan's largest life insurer, added: "At one point, there were definitely many problems. But it seems things have changed and there is a chance for success."
But Germany's participation was crucial for that success, insurance company investment managers and analysts said.

"Germany's power to influence things is expected to remain strong. Many (Japanese investors) may well be expecting Germany to take control," said Masayuki Kichikawa, senior economist at Nomura Research Institute.

Asahi Mutual is currently working with the scenario of initial EMU members in 1999 being Germany, France, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, with a later entry by one or two other countries, a view largely shared by Nippon Life.

The view is that this composition would lead to a strong, or "hard", Euro currency, while membership by countries such as Italy and Spain is seen leading to a "soft", or weaker, Euro, market participants say.

In terms of post-EMU investment, the Asahi manager said he feels equities could well be more exciting than bonds. "The good news (for bonds) is already in the market. Spreads will reduce and yield curves will steepen."
"We are taking uncertainty as a given and it's a critical point for profitability, but it does make (bond) investment difficult, and risks are likely to get much higher," he added.
The Nippon Life official said they expect investment in both Euro stocks and bonds to be profitable, although he warned that it was still much too early to predict trends.
"There will be three big currencies then -- the dollar, Euro and yen -- and some diversification will definitely be necessary," he said.
